title: Add in-layer MoE dropless fallback (moe_in_layer_dropless_fallback)
body:
Adds an in-layer alternative to retry_when_tokens_dropped. Each ring-of-experts MoE layer predicts from the router top-k (local tokens + a [chunks, EP] psum, all-reduced over the mesh) whether its ragged buffer would overflow, then uses lax.cond to run either the normal capped path or a chunked, fully rematerialized dropless path whose per-chunk buffer is no larger than the capped buffer.

Unlike the step-level retry, this never replays the train step, keeps state donation enabled, and needs no per-step host sync. The two options are mutually exclusive. The number of layers that took the dropless branch is logged as learning/moe_dropless_fallback_layers.

title: Fix GDN sequence-packing, head-CP sharding, and kernel config validation edge cases
body:
## Overview

Follow-up to merged PRs #5344, #5364, and #5386. During post-merge verification of Qwen3-Next / Qwen3.5 Gated Delta Net (GDN) sequence packing, context parallelism (`gdn_cp_mode="head"` / `"seq"`), and the Pallas TPU forward/backward kernels, we identified several configuration traps, sharding/gradient bugs, and numerical/runtime edge cases.

This PR resolves each of those issues and adds fast-fail configuration checks in `pyconfig` (`MaxTextConfig` and `RLConfig`). Comprehensive CPU, 1-chip TPU v7x, and 4-chip TPU v7x correctness and performance/HBM verification was conducted on Google3 Forge via companion CL **[http://cl/971437186](http://cl/971437186)** (to keep the unit tests in this repo lightweight and fast).

---

## Bugs Identified & How They Are Fixed

### 1. Configuration Validation & Fast-Fail Guards (`src/maxtext/configs/types.py`, `src/maxtext/utils/maxtext_utils.py`)

* **Silent cross-document state leakage when `use_gdn_kernel=True` with packed sequences and `enable_gdn_sequence_packing=False`:**
  * *Issue:* `enable_gdn_sequence_packing` defaults to `False`. Previously, running the Pallas GDN kernel with packed data while leaving `enable_gdn_sequence_packing=False` only logged a one-time warning in `MaxTextConfig` (and did not check `RLConfig` or `max_seq_token_per_tpu > 0`), allowing the kernel to ignore `decoder_segment_ids` and leak `conv1d` taps and recurrent state across packed documents.
  * *Fix:* Replaced the warning with a `ValueError` in `validate_gdn_config`, invoked by both `MaxTextConfig` (when `packing=True`) and `RLConfig` (when `max_seq_token_per_tpu > 0` or `packing=True` without `max_seq_token_per_tpu`). (The pure-JAX path `use_gdn_kernel=False` always honors `decoder_segment_ids` and is unaffected.)
* **Duplicate GDN computation and memory under Tensor Parallelism (`TP > 1`) with `use_gdn_kernel=True`:**
  * *Issue:* The Pallas GDN kernel `shard_map` partition specs do not shard heads along the `tensor` mesh axis (`P(mesh_batch, cp_axis_name, None)`), causing every TP rank to redundantly compute and store all GDN heads when `TP > 1`.
  * *Fix:* Added a fast-fail `ValueError` in both `MaxTextConfig` and `RLConfig` when `use_gdn_kernel=True` and `ici_tensor_parallelism * dcn_tensor_parallelism > 1`.
* **Unsupported kernel shapes (`gdn_chunk_size != 64`, head dims not multiples of `128`, unaligned per-rank sequence lengths) and `use_qk_norm_in_gdn=False`:**
  * *Issue:* When `use_gdn_kernel=True` was configured with `gdn_chunk_size != 64`, `gdn_key_head_dim % 128 != 0`, or `gdn_value_head_dim % 128 != 0`, the forward pass fell back to pure JAX while the backward pass fell back to slow Pallas interpret mode. When the per-rank sequence length (`max_target_length // cp` or `max_seq_token_per_tpu // cp`) was not a multiple of `gdn_chunk_size`, the forward fallback crashed inside `_compute_forward_conv_and_states` during chunk reshaping. Additionally, the TPU forward kernel always normalized `q` and `k` even if `use_qk_norm_in_gdn=False`.
  * *Fix:* `validate_gdn_config` now fast-fails up front in both `MaxTextConfig` and `RLConfig` unless `gdn_chunk_size == 64`, `gdn_key_head_dim % 128 == 0`, `gdn_value_head_dim % 128 == 0`, `(seq_len // cp) % gdn_chunk_size == 0`, and `use_qk_norm_in_gdn == True`. Also added a runtime guard at the top of `gdn_decoupled_conv1d` (`api.py`) for direct callers, and wired `use_qk_norm_in_gdn` through the forward kernel (`config.py`, `wrapper.py`, `compute_gdn.py`, `api.py`).
* **Overlapping granular GDN remat tensor groups & missing `ShardMode.EXPLICIT` + CP guard:**
  * *Issue:* `_expand_gdn_remat_names` (`maxtext_utils.py`) placed overlapping checkpoint names in `gdn`, `gdn_conv`, and `gdn_states`, so mixing `"device"` and `"offload"` across `gdn` and `gdn_conv` crashed at model build time (`ValueError: names should be exclusive`). Setting `gdn*` remat options without `remat_policy="custom"` was also silently ignored, and `ShardMode.EXPLICIT` with `cp > 1` bypassed validation when `use_gdn_kernel=True` (crashing later in head-CP `shard_map`).
  * *Fix:* Partitioned `_GDN_CONV_NAMES`, `_GDN_STATE_NAMES`, and `_GDN_OTHER_NAMES` into disjoint sets (`gdn` expands to the union of all three), added fast-fail checks when `gdn* != "remat"` without `remat_policy="custom"` or when `tensors_on_device` and `tensors_to_offload` intersect, removed the `not self.use_gdn_kernel` exemption on the `ShardMode.EXPLICIT` + CP check, and typed `gdn_cp_mode` as `Literal["auto", "seq", "head"]`.

---

### 2. Pure-JAX Head-Sharded Context Parallelism (`gdn_cp_mode="head"`) Gradient & TP Sharding Fix (`src/maxtext/kernels/gdn/model_runner.py`)

* **Corrupted `norm.rms_norm.scale` / `out_proj` gradients under pure-JAX `gdn_cp_mode="head"` with data parallelism (`data > 1`) and unsharded `tensor` axis (`TP > 1`):**
  * *Issue:* In `run_jax_gdn_delta_rule`, `gdn_cp_mode="head"` returned `core_attn_out` still sharded along the head axis (`P(mesh_batch, None, cp_axis, None)`) rather than sequence-sharded (`P(mesh_batch, cp_axis, mesh_head, None)`). When `data > 1`, feeding this head-sharded layout directly into the downstream gated RMSNorm and `out_proj` produced corrupted gradients on `norm.rms_norm.scale` and `out_proj.kernel`. In addition, `gdn_cp_mode="head"` did not include the `tensor` axis in its head sharding spec when `TP > 1`.
  * *Fix:* In `run_jax_gdn_delta_rule`:
    1. Sharded heads across the combined `(*head_tuple, *cp_tuple)` axes inside `shard_mapped_delta_rule`.
    2. Added `jax.lax.all_to_all` at the end of `shard_mapped_delta_rule` to return `core_attn_out` to sequence sharding (`P(mesh_batch, cp_axis_for_pspec, mesh_head, None)`), matching the kernel head-CP contract.
    3. Unified `gdn_cp_mode="auto"` resolution (`_resolve_gdn_cp_mode`: selects `"head"` at `cp == 2` when divisible and `"seq"` at `cp >= 4`) and the `context_parallel_load_balance=False` guard across both the kernel and pure-JAX runners.

---

### 3. Pallas TPU Kernel Forward, Backward & Context-Parallel Fixes (`src/maxtext/kernels/gdn/**`, `src/maxtext/models/qwen3.py`)

* **Eliminate unnecessary final-state gradient collectives in training (`api.py`, `model_runner.py`):**
  * *Issue:* Setting `symbolic_zeros=False` on `gdn_decoupled_conv1d.defvjp` and allocating zero initial states during `MODEL_MODE_TRAIN` caused every training step to materialize zero final-state cotangents (`d_next_conv_state`, `d_next_recurrent_state`) and execute an unnecessary cross-chip `jax.lax.psum` (~4 MiB/layer) under sequence-sharded CP.
  * *Fix:* Restored `symbolic_zeros=True` on `gdn_decoupled_conv1d.defvjp` (`api.py`) and pass `None` initial states during `MODEL_MODE_TRAIN` (`model_runner.py`). For unjitted eager calls (`if not isinstance(qkv, jax.core.Tracer)`), `shard_mapped_gdn` is wrapped in `jax.jit` so `shard_map` + `custom_vjp(symbolic_zeros=True)` works in eager mode while keeping the jitted training jaxpr and StableHLO 100% unchanged.
* **Target-platform dispatch for CPU-host AOT compilation (`runtime_utils.py`, `api.py`, `pallas_mosaic_tpu_bwd.py`):**
  * *Issue:* Forward and backward kernel dispatch checked `jax.extend.backend.get_backend().platform == "cpu"`, which caused CPU-host AOT compilation targeting a TPU mesh to lower the pure-JAX / interpret-mode fallback instead of the Pallas TPU kernels.
  * *Fix:* Added `target_platform(*arrays)` in `runtime_utils.py` (inspecting array sharding devices, active mesh devices, or default device platform). When `target_platform == "tpu"`, both forward and backward lower the Pallas Mosaic TPU kernels and raise a `ValueError` if given unsupported shapes instead of falling back to interpret mode.
* **Right-padded prefill `next_conv_state` & 1-token autoregressive decode (`model_runner.py`, `qwen3.py`):**
  * *Issue:* When `enable_gdn_sequence_packing=False`, `run_gdn_kernel_layer` dropped `decoder_segment_ids` before extracting `next_conv_state`, causing right-padded prefill prompts to save trailing `0`-padding tokens into the conv state cache instead of the last `K-1` valid prompt tokens. Additionally, 1-token `MODEL_MODE_AUTOREGRESSIVE` decode with `use_gdn_kernel=True` entered the chunked kernel path and failed chunk-size validation.
  * *Fix:* Preserved `raw_segment_ids` in `run_gdn_kernel_layer` so `extract_segment_conv_state` always extracts the last `K-1` valid tokens after prefill, and routed 1-token `MODEL_MODE_AUTOREGRESSIVE` decode (`seq_len == 1`) in `qwen3.py` to the pure-JAX recurrent step (`jax_ar_gated_delta_rule`).
* **Numerical precision, segment-ID canonicalization & SMEM/DMA fixes:**
  * *Float32 intra-chunk log-decay cumsum (`compute_gdn.py`):* Always accumulate `g_cum_sum_list` and compute `g_cum[i] - g_cum[j]` in `float32` before `jnp.exp`, preventing catastrophic cancellation when `gdn_state_dtype=bfloat16`.
  * *Float32 post-conv keys in CP pass 1 (`compute_conv1d_bwd.py`, `api.py`):* Added `output_dtype=jnp.float32` to `conv1d_silu_fwd` during CP pass-1 `compose_local_from_t_inv` so `m_local` matches `s_ext`'s `float32` precision.
  * *Zero-norm `q`/`k` guard in backward kernel (`pallas_mosaic_tpu_bwd.py`):* Masked `dq` and `dk` to zero when $\lVert q\rVert^2 \le 10^{-30}$ or $\lVert k\rVert^2 \le 10^{-30}$, matching `qwen3._l2norm`'s forward guard on padded/zero rows.
  * *Direct-caller segment-ID canonicalization (`wrapper.py`, `api.py`, `pallas_mosaic_tpu_bwd.py`):* Added `canonicalize_local_segment_ids` so direct kernel callers passing raw non-monotonic IDs (`[1, 2, 1]`) or IDs $> 2^{24}$ automatically canonicalize to `1..N` and align `init_seg`.
  * *SMEM repeat-table sizing & decode DMA indexing (`metadata.py`, `wrapper.py`, `memory_ref.py`, `tiling.py`):* Sized SMEM repeat tables by chunk count ($\lceil N_{\text{tokens}} / C \rceil + N_{\text{reqs}} + 2$, 64× smaller in prefill), fixed decode DMA indexing `p_id * seq_tile_size + idx` in `memory_ref.py`, clamped `decode_tile_size` to `num_seqs` in `tiling.py`, vectorized per-chunk conv halo construction in `wrapper.py`, and removed dead monkey-patches/branches in `runtime_utils.py` and `model_runner.py`.

---

## Verification & Benchmarks (Executed on Google3 Forge CPU & TPU v7x via `cl/971437186`)

All full-scale CPU, 1-chip TPU v7x, and 4-chip TPU v7x (`2x2`) unit, multi-chip context-parallel, and performance/HBM tests were executed on Google3 Forge using companion CL **[http://cl/971437186](http://cl/971437186)** (**[sponge2/e8fcbdd8-f1d0-42be-9c69-73250d2fc526](http://sponge2/e8fcbdd8-f1d0-42be-9c69-73250d2fc526)** and **[sponge2/293ff9f0-c40c-4e6d-b152-e9054f3c44a0](http://sponge2/293ff9f0-c40c-4e6d-b152-e9054f3c44a0)**). title: Exclude cuda-bindings and CUTLASS DSL from decoupled requirements
body:
# Description

`decoupled-requirements.txt` is meant to install on any hardware (its header says the accelerator wheels are left out "so the file installs on any hardware"), but it currently fails to resolve on macOS:

```
error: No solution found when resolving dependencies
  cause: Because cuda-bindings>=13.4.2 has no wheels with a matching platform tag (e.g., `macosx_13_0_arm64`) and you require cuda-bindings>=13.4.2, we can conclude that your requirements are unsatisfiable.
```

The cuda12 lock now pulls in `cuda-bindings` and `nvidia-cutlass-dsl*` (including a `-cu13` variant), and `generate_decoupled_requirements.py` does not match them: its accelerator filters only cover `nvidia-cuda-*`, `nvidia-cudnn-*` and `*-cu12`. `cuda-bindings` 13.4.2 ships only `manylinux` and `win` wheels, so the lock is unsatisfiable on macOS. CI runs on Linux only, so this did not show up there.

This PR:
- adds `cuda-bindings` and `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` to `EXCLUDED_ACCELERATOR_PREFIXES` and `-cu13` to `EXCLUDED_ACCELERATOR_SUFFIXES`, and updates the comment explaining what is kept and why;
- regenerates `decoupled-requirements.txt` with the script (5 lines removed, nothing else changes).

The excluded packages now appear in `--print-accelerator-requirements`, so a GPU run of the decoupled suite still installs them on top, as with the other CUDA libraries. `cuda-pathfinder` is intentionally kept: it is a pure-Python wheel (`cuda_pathfinder-1.8.2-py3-none-any.whl`) and resolves everywhere, like `nvidia-ml-py`.

No code in `src/` or `tests/` imports `cutlass` or `cuda.bindings`, so dropping them from the decoupled environment does not affect the `decoupled_target` tests.

# Tests

Resolution of the decoupled file before and after, with `uv pip compile --python-version 3.12 --python-platform <platform> --resolution=lowest`:

| Platform | Before (`main`) | After (this PR) |
|---|---|---|
| `aarch64-apple-darwin` | fails (`cuda-bindings` has no wheel) | resolves, 208 packages |
| `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` | resolves, 214 packages | resolves, 208 packages |
| `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` | resolves, 214 packages | resolves, 208 packages |

On Linux the only packages that drop out are the five excluded ones plus `nvidia-cutlass-dsl-libs-cu12`, which was only pulled in by `nvidia-cutlass-dsl`.

Also checked:
- `python3 src/dependencies/scripts/generate_decoupled_requirements.py --check` passes on the regenerated file.
- `--print-accelerator-requirements` now lists `cuda-bindings` and `nvidia-cutlass-dsl*`.
- `pylint --rcfile=pylintrc` (10.00/10) and `pyink --pyink-indentation=2 --line-length=122 --check` pass on the changed script.
- End to end on an arm64 Mac: installed the decoupled environment, installed MaxText with `--no-deps`, and ran a 5-step `dataset_type=synthetic` pre-training job on CPU with an 8-device host mesh (`--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=8`, `DECOUPLE_GCLOUD=TRUE`); it completes with loss decreasing 5.987 → 5.976.

title: [MaxTextEngine] Fix model build and sharding, add optimizer offload and GRPO AOT compile, match train.py speed on TPU
body:
# Description

This PR makes `MaxTextTrainingEngine`, the trainer that Tunix's RL stack drives one micro-batch at a time, work
correctly at large sharded configurations such as the Qwen3.5-397B-A17B MLPerf trainer config (`custom_mesh_and_rule=cp-as-ep`).
It fixes model construction and sharding-rule handling, implements `optimizer_memory_host_offload` (previously ignored by
the engine), adds a `grad_accumulation_dtype` option, fixes mid-step checkpoint resume, turns the engine's ahead-of-time
compile tool into a per-kernel device-memory report that can also compile Tunix's GRPO loss from the command line, updates
the standalone trainer script, and adds a README with instructions and a full recipe to run all of it.

It also closes the throughput gap to `pre_train/train.py`: on 128 TPU v7x chips at the Qwen3.5-397B-A17B configuration the
engine now runs at 201.43 s/step (2,603 tokens/s/chip) against `pre_train/train.py`'s 206.12 s/step (2,544 tokens/s/chip),
and trains with float32 gradients at 217.19 s/step (see Tests).

Before this change, the engine could not be constructed at `cp-as-ep` when the caller had set a mesh, several entry points
traced the model without MaxText's logical axis rules (Tunix binds none), the offload flags were silently ignored, and the
AOT tool could not compile Qwen3.5 or Tunix losses.

BUGS: b/565501755

## Why, and what changed

### 1. Model construction under a caller's mesh
**Problem.** The engine builds the model with flax's `nnx.eval_shape`. When the caller had set a mesh with `jax.set_mesh`,
flax re-derived shardings from logical axis names and raised on valid MaxText rule sets (at `cp-as-ep`:
`Resource axis: norm of P('norm',) is not found in mesh`). Without any rules bound, Tokamax ring attention fails instead,
because it validates its sequence sharding when the layer is constructed.
**Fix.** `_build_model` binds MaxText's logical axis rules and clears the mesh (`jax.set_mesh(None)`) for the duration of
construction. This works whether the caller uses `jax.set_mesh`, the legacy `with mesh:` (what Tunix does), or no mesh.

### 2. Sharding rules at every traced entry point
**Problem.** Tunix constructs and calls the engine under `with mesh:` only, with no logical axis rules. Entry points that
traced the model inherited whatever the caller had bound; `eval_step`, for example, traced outside the rules.
**Fix.** `fwd_bwd`, `update`, `eval_step` and `fwd_only` each enter `_sharding_ctx()` (mesh + logical axis rules)
themselves. New `model_scope(*inputs)` implements Tunix's `AbstractTrainer.model_scope`: it yields the live model and the
inputs placed on the mesh, under the rules, which Tunix's `TrainerWorker.per_token_logps` uses to score log-probs with the
trainer's weights. A `logical_axis_rules_for_eval` that differs from the training rules now raises instead of being
silently ignored.

### 3. Optimizer host offload
**Problem.** The engine never read `optimizer_memory_host_offload`: the optimizer moments always stayed in device memory,
which matters most at the forward/backward peak. `parameter_memory_host_offload` was also silently ignored.
**Fix.** With `optimizer_memory_host_offload=true`, the optimizer state lives in `pinned_host` memory between updates.
`update` moves it to the device for the optimizer arithmetic, and the kernel's output shardings return it to host memory,
mirroring what `pre_train/train.py` does. The forward/backward kernels never take the optimizer state, so it is no longer
resident during them. The placement is re-applied after a checkpoint restore, after the state setters, and on the eager
(uncompiled) path. Zero-1 (`shard_optimizer_over_data`) keeps the host memory kind. `parameter_memory_host_offload=true`
now raises `NotImplementedError` rather than doing nothing.

### 4. Gradient accumulation dtype
**Before.** Each micro-batch's gradients were cast to `grad_dtype` and summed in `grad_dtype`.
**Now.** New config key `grad_accumulation_dtype` (`""` by default, which keeps the previous behaviour). `"float32"` sums
micro-batch gradients in float32 and casts to `grad_dtype` once, after dividing by the total denominator; for float32
weights this is `pre_train/train.py`'s order and matches it bit for bit in the CPU parity test. The trade-off is a float32
accumulator kept on device between micro-batches, which is why it is opt-in. The division by the accumulated denominator
now happens in float32 (previously a bf16 division rounded the token count).

### 5. Mid-step checkpoint resume
**Problem.** The accumulator's restore target was built from the parameters, so a checkpoint saved between micro-batches
came back in `weight_dtype`. When that differs from the accumulation dtype (the default bf16 grads with float32 weights),
the compiled kernels rejected it (`Argument types differ from the types for which this computation was compiled`), and on
the lazily compiled path the step silently recompiled with a float32 accumulator.
**Fix.** `CheckpointState.accumulated_grads_target` restores the accumulator in the accumulation dtype with the parameter
shardings, and the engine casts defensively after restore.

### 6. AOT compile tool (`maxtext_engine_compile.py`)
**Problem.** `AbstractMaxTextEngine` traced the model graph under a mesh and failed on the same configurations as (1), so it
could not compile Qwen3.5 or losses written for Tunix. Its output was the raw `memory_analysis()` of each kernel, which is
easy to misread: the forward/backward kernels do not take the optimizer state as an argument, yet it stays in device memory
while they run.
**Fix.** The abstract engine traces the model the way the live engine builds it (and wraps it in the Tunix adapter when
asked). The tool prints each kernel's memory analysis and a per-device table: `resident = arg + out - alias + temp`, plus
the train state that stays in device memory without being a kernel argument, with host memory reported separately. The last
line, `TRAIN-KERNEL DEVICE PEAK`, is the largest total over the three kernels, and the legend lists what it does not cover
(weight-sync staging, `fwd_only` scoring, the eval kernel, anything the caller holds). A `WEIGHT-SYNC STAGING` line
estimates the weight-sync copy when `use_weight_converter=false`. Compiled executables are saved before the report is
printed, so a report error cannot lose them.

### 7. Standalone trainer script (`experimental/maxtext_engine/train.py`)
- Constructs and drives the engine the way Tunix does, with no outer `logical_axis_rules`. The previous outer wrap hid
  missing bindings inside the engine.
- Splits each global batch into micro-batches in `pre_train/train.py`'s order (micro-batch k = rows `k::G`), in one jitted
  call, so every device keeps its own rows and the split needs no collectives.
- Reports `Tokens/s/device` and `Tokens/s/chip`. The old per-chip number divided by the device count, which halves it on
  TPUs with two devices per chip.
- Logs memory after compile and after the first step, and times each step from dispatch until its device work drains.

### 8. Gradient accumulation kernel
**Problem.** Every micro-batch after the first ran a second forward/backward program that took the donated gradient sum as
an input. XLA folded the add into the token embedding's gradient scatter-add, which gathers an unsharded copy of that leaf
at the program's peak; on large configurations this pushed the program past the scheduler's memory limit and cost
compute/communication overlap, so the accumulating micro-steps ran slower than the first one.
**Fix.** Every micro-batch runs the same `fwd_bwd` program, and a new donated `accumulate` kernel adds each later
micro-batch's gradients and loss denominator into the running sums. The forward/backward program is compiled once instead
of twice. The trade-off: each micro-batch's gradients now sit beside the running sum until `accumulate` adds them, so
`fwd_bwd`'s peak holds one more gradient tree (two float32 trees with `grad_accumulation_dtype=float32`). That lowers the
peak only where XLA's fold was expensive, as at the Qwen3.5-397B configuration, where a TPU v7x run confirmed the speed-up;
on smaller configurations the peak rises by one gradient tree.
The accumulated gradients are unchanged bit for bit except the token-embedding leaf, which is now summed in source order
(`acc + grads`) instead of the order XLA's fold chose, so it can differ by rounding.

### 9. Casting all-reduced gradients after the all-reduce (`cast_grads_after_all_reduce`, default off)
**Problem.** Gradients are cast to the accumulation dtype inside `fwd_bwd`. For parameters sharded over none of the axes a
batch is split over (norm scales and similar), XLA can sink that cast into the backward loop and turn their
cross-device all-reduces into synchronous bf16 reductions; on the TPU configuration we profiled, this reduced how much of
the backward pass's collective time was hidden behind compute.
**Fix.** With the new key on, those gradients leave `fwd_bwd` in the parameters' dtype and are cast when they join the
running sum, after the all-reduce. Selection is by sharding, not size. With the key off, the compiled kernels are unchanged.
It is meant for TPU together with the libtpu flag `--xla_tpu_enable_offloading_copy_to_sparsecore=false`, which keeps
layout copies off the SparseCore that the backward pass's collectives also use; alone, the key can raise device memory.
The flag raises device memory too, so both are documented as per-configuration choices to check with the memory report.
With both at the Qwen3.5-397B configuration on TPU v7x, the engine ran 2.3% faster than `pre_train/train.py` (see Tests).

### 10. Compiling with Tunix's GRPO loss from the command line
`maxtext_engine_compile` could compile a Tunix loss only through its Python API. The new key `compile_engine_loss=grpo`
sets up the abstract engine as Tunix's RL trainer sets up a live one: the model behind `TunixMaxTextAdapter`, and the loss
and input mapping from Tunix's `GRPOAdapter`. `compile_engine_grpo_config` passes the trainer's `GRPOConfig` options and
`compile_engine_logps_chunk_size` computes log-probabilities in chunks as `TrainerWorker` does, so the memory report can
match a real RL trainer. With the default (`maxtext`), the tool compiles what it compiled before.

The micro-batch it compiles for is built by Tunix's own code, as its orchestrator builds one:
`GRPOAdapter.create_trainer_payloads`, the batch assembler `create_batch_assembler` picks, the reference model's
log-probabilities when the loss needs them, and the fields Tunix's sampler-trainer agreement step writes (with
`sampler_is: token`, `sampler_is_weights`).
- `compile_engine_max_seq_token_per_tpu` and `compile_engine_max_segments_per_packed_row` (Tunix's `max_seq_token_per_tpu`
  and `max_segments_per_packed_row`) compile for `SequencePackedBatchAssembler`'s packed rows, one per device of the
  mesh's data, fsdp, fsdp_transpose and expert axes, which sends Tunix's loss down its per-segment aggregation.
- `compile_engine_router_replay` has the rollouts return their MoE routing, which the micro-batch carries as
  `routed_experts` (`[sequences, tokens, layers, top_k]` int16) wherever Tunix's assembler carries it. Tunix's packed
  assembler currently leaves it out, and the tool says so when the micro-batch it compiles has no routing.
The GRPO options are rejected, rather than ignored, without `compile_engine_loss=grpo`.

### 11. Documentation
Adds `src/maxtext/training_engine/README.md`: how to run the standalone script, how to use the engine from Python, how to run
the AOT memory report (also with Tunix's GRPO loss) and the tests; "Running fast on TPU" (the libtpu flag,
`cast_grads_after_all_reduce`, float32 gradients, profiling a large step within the profiler's trace-size limit); a full
Qwen3.5-397B-A17B recipe for 128 TPU v7x chips with bfloat16 and float32 variants and the memory check; the TPU v7x results;
the flow of one optimizer step, the sharding rules, the config keys the engine honours, and how to read the memory report.

## Relationship to #5371
This PR includes the three commits of the first revision of #5371 unchanged, because the work here builds on them.
#5371 has since added its own optimizer host offload; this PR's implementation (section 3) is the one covered by the tests
below, so only one of the two should land.

## Shortcomings and possible future improvements
- **Auxiliary losses under gradient accumulation.** With more than one micro-batch, `pre_train/train.py` adds auxiliary
  losses (MoE load balancing, MTP, indexer) to the unnormalized cross-entropy sum before dividing by the token count, which
  scales them down; the engine weights them as `pre_train/train.py` does without accumulation. When these losses are enabled,
  the engine's logged loss and perplexity also include them. All are off by default (for example
  `load_balance_loss_weight: 0.0`).
- **Routed-bias updates** (used by some DeepSeek configs) are not applied by the engine; such configs should be rejected
  explicitly.
- **Throughput.** Matching `pre_train/train.py` on large TPU configurations needs the libtpu flag and
  `cast_grads_after_all_reduce` (section 9), which are opt-in because they can raise device memory.
- The AOT report's peak covers the three training kernels only; with the default `use_weight_converter=true` the weight-sync
  copy is not estimated.

# Tests

**Unit and end-to-end tests on CPU** (JAX 0.11.1, Tunix on `PYTHONPATH`):

```bash
JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu python3 -m pytest tests/post_training/unit/maxtext_engine_*test.py \
  tests/post_training/unit/router_replay_engine_test.py
```

New and extended tests, all in `tests/post_training/unit/`:

| test file | what it checks |
|---|---|
| `maxtext_engine_test.py` | optimizer offload placement (host between updates, device during `update`), identical numbers with and without offload, re-offload after restore and after the state setters, the eager path; `parameter_memory_host_offload` and differing eval rules are rejected; model build binds the rules and clears the caller's mesh; `eval_step` traces under the rules; `model_scope`; accumulation dtypes and the float32 denominator; Zero-1 keeps the memory kind |
| `maxtext_engine_model_build_test.py` | constructs a scaled-down Qwen3.5-397B at `cp-as-ep` on 8 CPU devices under `jax.set_mesh`, `with mesh:` and no mesh |
| `maxtext_engine_checkpoint_test.py` | a step resumed from a mid-step Orbax checkpoint is bit-identical to the uninterrupted step, across weight / grad / accumulation dtype combinations, compiled and lazily compiled |
| `maxtext_engine_compile_test.py` | the memory report against real XLA compiles, including donation, host memory, optimizer offload, Zero-1 on 4 devices and the weight-sync estimate; `compile_engine_loss=grpo` with Tunix's GRPO loss on the payload Tunix builds (padded and packed, compared with Tunix's assemblers; router replay; the sampler-trainer agreement fields, compared with Tunix's own step), the trainer's `GRPOConfig` options and log-probability chunking |
| `maxtext_engine_compile_parity_test.py` | the abstract engine compiles a tiny Qwen3.5 (scanned, MoE, Tunix adapter) to the same StableHLO, optimized HLO and memory analysis as the live engine, under the default rules and `cp-as-ep` |
| `maxtext_engine_grad_cast_test.py` | `cast_grads_after_all_reduce`: selection by sharding and dtype, casting after the all-reduce, and the deferred data-parallel all-reduce left alone |
| `maxtext_engine_train_test.py` | the standalone script end to end (with accumulation, with offload), the Tunix path through Tunix's own builders and `TrainerWorker.per_token_logps`, and parity with `pre_train/train.py`: loss within 1e-5 and updates within 1e-4 (float32) / 3e-4 (bf16) |

Results on the final tree: the engine suites pass 138 tests (the same 4 failures as the base branch, listed below), the
new test files pass (model build, mid-step checkpoint, compile parity, gradient cast), the script and parity suite passes
4 of 4, the compile tool's 63 of 63 with 37 subtests (including the GRPO path, packing and router replay), and the config tests 179 of 179. With the accumulate kernel, five of the six parity cases stay bit-exact; the all-float32 AdamW case
moves from exact to within its unchanged gate, because the token-embedding gradient is now summed in source order rather than
in the order XLA's fold chose (the same fold `pre_train/train.py` gets). The existing engine suites give the same results with and without this change; the same three
tests and one packing subtest fail on the base branch as well (`test_maybe_register_pathways_persistence`, two profiling
tests and `small_pack`). With `cast_grads_after_all_reduce` off, the compiled kernels are unchanged. The config tests
(`tests/unit/configs_test.py`, `configs_value_test.py`, `pyconfig_test.py`) pass. pyink and pylint report no new
findings on the changed files.

**On TPU v7x**, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B at the MLPerf trainer configuration: 128 chips (256 devices), fsdp 32 x context 4 x
expert 2 with `cp-as-ep`, sequence length 65,536, 1,024 sequences per step (16 micro-batches of 64), float32 weights,
bfloat16 compute, AdamW. The engine rows ran this PR's code with the standalone script; steady state over the steps after
step 0 (spread under 0.1 s). The full flags are in the README's recipe.

| trainer | settings | s/step | tokens/s/chip | vs `pre_train/train.py` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pre_train/train.py` | bfloat16 gradients | 206.12 | 2,543.6 | — |
| `pre_train/train.py` | + `--xla_tpu_enable_offloading_copy_to_sparsecore=false` | does not fit | — | runs out of device memory at load |

| engine | + `--xla_tpu_enable_offloading_copy_to_sparsecore=false` | 214.70 | 2,442 | 4.2% slower |
| engine | + `cast_grads_after_all_reduce=true` | **201.43** | **2,603** | **2.3% faster** |
| engine | float32 gradients, optimizer offload, `context=remat` | 229.72 | 2,282 | 11.4% slower |
| engine | float32 gradients, optimizer offload, `context=remat`, + the libtpu flag | 217.19 | 2,414 | 5.4% slower |

The `pre_train/train.py` rows ran with two kernel changes that are not part of MaxText yet (a single-scan vocabulary-tiled
loss and a cost estimate for the gated-delta-net forward kernel), which make it slightly faster; the engine rows ran
without them. `pre_train/train.py`'s step time is the interval between its metric lines. Before the accumulate kernel
(section 8), the engine's bfloat16 step was 228.97 s with those two kernel changes and 224.76 s after it.

To reproduce, use the recipe in `src/maxtext/training_engine/README.md` ("Recipe: Qwen3.5-397B-A17B on 128 TPU v7x chips").

title: Enable end-to-end GDN sequence packing across Conv1D, Pallas fwd/bwd kernels, and Context Parallelism
body:
## Summary This PR updates `atwigg/mlperf` with **end-to-end GDN Sequence Packing support** across both the **TPU Pallas Forward/Backward Kernels (`use_gdn_kernel=True`)** and the **Pure JAX Reference Path (`use_gdn_kernel=False`)**, following the modular `model_runner.py` architecture introduced in [#5344](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/pull/5344) and upgrading the Pure JAX sequence packing path from [#5351](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/pull/5351). --- ## Checklist - [x] Passes all `pre-commit` linters (`pyink`, `pylint`, `codespell`, `yamllint`) with zero warnings. - [x] Verified on CPU and Ghostfish v7x TPU (`-c opt`, 1-chip and 4-chip) across unit, CP, and Qwen3.5-397B `S=8192` benchmark suites (counts below). - [x] Verified 8-layer Qwen3.5-397B (`S=65536`, `gf=4x4x8`) `train_compile` program HBM with packing off vs. on. --- ## How Sequence Packing Works in GDN Unlike standard Softmax attention—where sequence packing only requires a block-diagonal `segment_ids[i] == segment_ids[j]` mask on the $QK^T$ scores—a **Gated Delta Net (`Qwen3NextGatedDeltaNet`)** has **two stateful stages** where tokens from an earlier sequence will leak into a later sequence unless explicitly isolated: 1. **Stage 1 — Causal 1D Depthwise Convolution (`Conv1D`, kernel size $K = 4$)**: Every token looks back at the previous 3 tokens (`[t-3, t-2, t-1, t]`). If a new sequence starts at token $t$, taps reaching into `t-1`, `t-2`, or `t-3` belong to the *previous* sequence and must be zeroed out in both the forward and backward passes. 2. **Stage 2 — Chunked Gated Delta Rule (`chunk_size = 64`)**: Tokens are processed in 64-token chunks while maintaining a running recurrent hidden state $S_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D_k \times D_v}$ from chunk to chunk. Within a chunk, tokens interact causally weighted by cumulative log-decay (`g_cumsum`). When multiple sequences are packed together, we must control both **intra-chunk token interactions** and **inter-chunk recurrent state ($S_t$) propagation**. ### Visual Timeline: 4 Packed Sequences Across 4 Chunks (`S = 256`, `chunk_size = 64`) Consider a 256-token packed row divided into **4 chunks of 64 tokens**, containing **4 packed sequences** with different alignment boundaries: - **`Seq 1` (`tokens 0..63`, length 64)**: Fills **Chunk 0** (`0..63`) exactly to the chunk boundary. - **`Seq 2` (`tokens 64..135`, length 72)**: Starts cleanly at **Chunk 1** (`64`), fills all of Chunk 1 (`64..127`), and spills 8 tokens into **Chunk 2** (`128..135`). - **`Seq 3` (`tokens 136..180`, length 45)**: Starts and ends **entirely inside Chunk 2** (`136..180`). - **`Seq 4` (`tokens 181..255`, length 75)**: Starts mid-way through **Chunk 2** (`181..191`) and continues through the end of **Chunk 3** (`192..255`). ``` Token Index: 0 63 | 64 127 | 128 135 136 180 181 191 | 192 255 +----------------------+-----------------------+---------+---------+---------+----------------------+ Sequence ID: | Seq 1 (len 64) | Seq 2 (part 1) | Seq 2 | Seq 3 | Seq 4 | Seq 4 (part 2) | +----------------------+-----------------------+---------+---------+---------+----------------------+ Chunk Index: Chunk 0 Chunk 1 Chunk 2 Chunk 3 [0 .. 63] [64 .. 127] [128 .. 191] [192 .. 255] ``` | Chunk | Token Range | Sequences in Chunk | Incoming State ($S_{\text{in}}$) | Intra-Chunk Computation (`Conv1D` + Chunked Delta Rule) | Outgoing State ($S_{\text{out}}$) Passed to Next Chunk | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Chunk 0** | `0 .. 63` | **`Seq 1`** (`0..63`) | Starts at $S_{\text{in}} = 0$. | All 64 tokens belong to `Seq 1`. Standard causal `Conv1D` and intra-chunk delta rule over `0..63`. | Accumulates all 64 tokens of `Seq 1` into $S_0$. | | **Chunk 1** | `64 .. 127` | **`Seq 2`** (`64..127`) | **Reset to $0$!** Even though $S_0$ arrives from Chunk 0, `token 63` (`Seq 1`) $\neq$ `token 64` (`Seq 2`), so $S_0$ is wiped (`m_keep = 0`). | Tokens `64, 65, 66` block `Conv1D` taps from `61, 62, 63` (`Seq 1`). All 64 tokens (`64..127`) belong to `Seq 2`. | Accumulates tokens `64..127` of `Seq 2` into $S_1$. | | **Chunk 2** | `128 .. 191` | **`Seq 2`** (`128..135`)
**`Seq 3`** (`136..180`)
**`Seq 4`** (`181..191`) | **Kept for `Seq 2` only!** Since `token 127` (`Seq 2`) $==$ `token 128` (`Seq 2`), $S_1$ is retained (`m_keep = 1`), but `m_in` applies $S_1$ **only** to tokens `128..135` (`Seq 2`), never to `Seq 3` or `Seq 4`. | Three disjoint islands inside one chunk (`128..135`, `136..180`, `181..191`). `Conv1D` taps and intra-chunk attention/decay are strictly blocked at `135->136` and `180->181`. | **Accumulates `Seq 4` (`181..191`) only!** `Seq 2` and `Seq 3` finished inside Chunk 2, so `m_out` selects only tokens matching Chunk 2's last token (`Seq 4` at `191`) to form $S_2$. | | **Chunk 3** | `192 .. 255` | **`Seq 4`** (`192..255`) | **Kept for `Seq 4`!** Since `token 191` (`Seq 4`) $==$ `token 192` (`Seq 4`), $S_2$ (carrying `181..191`) flows directly into all of Chunk 3 (`m_keep = 1`, `m_in = 1`). | Tokens `192, 193, 194` validly read `Conv1D` taps `189, 190, 191` from Chunk 2 because both belong to `Seq 4`. | Accumulates `Seq 4` (`181..255`) into final state $S_3$. | --- ## Edge Cases & How Each Is Handled 1. **Exact Chunk-Aligned Boundary (`Seq 1: 0..63` $\to$ `Seq 2: 64..135`)**: - When a sequence ends at the exact end of a chunk (`token 63`) and the next sequence starts at `token 64`, every token inside Chunk 0 has `m_out = 1` and every token inside Chunk 1 has `m_in = 1`. - To prevent `Seq 1`'s final state $S_0$ from leaking into `Seq 2`, we compare the last active sequence ID of Chunk 0 (`seg_prev = Seq 1`) against Chunk 1's sequence IDs. Because `Seq 1 != Seq 2`, the carry-over gate `m_keep` zeros out $S_0$ at the chunk boundary, and `Conv1D` masks out the 3-token halo (`61..63`). 2. **Sequence Crossing a Chunk Boundary and Ending Mid-Chunk (`Seq 2: 64..135`)**: - `Seq 2` crosses from Chunk 1 into Chunk 2 and ends at `token 135`. - At the start of Chunk 2, `m_keep = 1` preserves $S_1$, while the input state mask `m_in` (`seg_c == seg_c[0]`) is `True` only for tokens `128..135` and `False` for `136..191`. Thus $S_1$ updates `Seq 2`'s final 8 tokens and is invisible to `Seq 3` and `Seq 4`. 3. **Short Sequence Contained Entirely Within One Chunk (`Seq 3: 136..180`)**: - Because `Seq 3` starts after `token 128` and ends before `token 191`, both `m_in` (reads incoming state from Chunk 1) and `m_out` (writes outgoing state to Chunk 3) are `False` for every token in `Seq 3`. - `Seq 3` is solved purely within Chunk 2: its cumulative decay `g_cumsum` resets at `token 136`, and its $64 \times 64$ intra-chunk causal/strict masks (`seg_c[i] == seg_c[j]`) isolate `136..180` from both `Seq 2` (`128..135`) and `Seq 4` (`181..191`). 4. **Sequence Starting Mid-Chunk and Continuing to the Next Chunk (`Seq 4: 181..255`)**: - `Seq 4` begins at `token 181` inside Chunk 2 and continues into Chunk 3. - At the end of Chunk 2, the outgoing state mask `m_out` (`seg_c == seg_last_active`) is `True` **only** for tokens `181..191` (`Seq 4`), decaying and summing only `Seq 4`'s tokens into $S_2$ while discarding `Seq 2` and `Seq 3`. 5. **Mid-Row / Trailing `0`-Padding & Ultra-Short Sequences ($L < 4$ in `Conv1D`)**: - Packed rows often contain `0`-padding at the end of a row (or between segments). If `0`-padding were treated as a regular segment ID, a sequence ending right before trailing zeros at a chunk boundary would appear to change segment IDs (`Seq k -> 0`) and lose its state, or padding tokens could corrupt running sums. - We encode segment IDs (`encode_segment_ids`) using an associative scan that preserves the **last active sequence ID** with a negative sign (`-d`) on padding positions (`+d` on valid tokens). Padding tokens (`s_enc <= 0`) have their `Conv1D` outputs, gates (`g`, `beta`), and attention outputs zeroed out, while `abs(s_enc)` carries the active sequence identity across padding gaps without corrupting $S_t$. - For sequences shorter than the `Conv1D` window ($L \in \{1, 2, 3\}$), each tap $k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ checks `(seg_id[t] == seg_id[t - k]) & (seg_id[t] > 0)` in both forward and backward passes (and masks `dz` before shifting in backward `conv1d_silu_bwd`), guaranteeing zero cross-sequence bleed. 6. **Context Parallelism (`cp_size > 1` in both `head` and `seq` Modes)**: - When a packed sequence is sharded across multiple TPU chips (`cp_size > 1`), sequences and `Conv1D` 3-token halos can straddle chip boundaries. - Both the Pallas kernel path (`cp_gdn.py`) and Pure JAX path (`gdn_cp.py`) exchange the 3-token `Conv1D` segment halo and apply segment-aware inter-chunk state composition (`m_keep`, `m_in`, `m_out`) across TPU sub-chunks, ensuring bitwise-equivalent results whether `cp_size = 1`, `2`, or `4`. --- ## Improvements to Pure JAX + Sequence Packing Over PR #5351 We also upgraded the **Pure JAX + Sequence Packing (`use_gdn_kernel=False`)** implementation relative to [#5351](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/pull/5351): 1. **Clean Modularization Matching [#5344](https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/pull/5344)**: - Extracted `segmented_causal_depthwise_conv1d`, `prepare_jax_gdn_segment_masks`, and `run_jax_gdn_delta_rule` into `src/maxtext/kernels/gdn/model_runner.py` and delegated from `src/maxtext/models/qwen3.py` (while keeping backward compatibility with `#5351`'s 4-argument helper signature). 2. **Full Context Parallelism (`cp_size > 1`) Support in Pure JAX**: - In `#5351`, Pure JAX sequence packing only applied when `cp_size == 1` (the `cp_size > 1` `shard_map` path did not pass `segment_ids`). Our Pure JAX path supports **both** `head`-sharded CP (`all_to_all`) and `seq`-sharded CP (`gdn_cp.custom_chunk_gated_delta_rule` with cross-chip `Conv1D` halo + segment-aware `compose_local`). 3. **Memory-Efficient `bfloat16` Per-Tap `Conv1D` Slicing**: - Keeps the padded `Conv1D` input in `bfloat16` before slicing each tap and accumulates the 4 masked tap products in `float32`, cutting temporary `Conv1D` tensor memory in half compared to upcasting the entire padded tensor upfront. 4. **Mid-Row & Trailing `0`-Padding State Preservation**: - Uses `encode_segment_ids` (`+d` / `-d`) in `prepare_jax_gdn_segment_masks` and `gdn_cp.py` so mid-row or trailing `0`-padding never corrupts state propagation across chunks. --- ## CLI Flags to Enable To enable GDN sequence packing in training or compilation runs, pass: ```yaml packing: true enable_gdn_sequence_packing: true use_gdn_kernel: true # True = TPU Pallas Fwd/Bwd kernels; False = Pure JAX reference path gdn_cp_mode: "auto" # Supports "auto", "head", and "seq" with cp_size >= 1 ``` --- ## Review Fixes in This Revision Commit `2ca3dbbb` fixes these sequence-packing correctness issues: - More than 256 segment IDs. - `seg_ids=ones` vs unpacked parity. - Packed CP in `head` and `seq` modes. - State continuity across chunks and shards. title: [MaxTextEngine] Fix Qwen3.5-397B MLPerf 6.1 standalone trainer harness, MoE aux loss parity, and optimizer host offload (b/565501755)
body:
# Description

1. `src/maxtext/training_engine/maxtext_engine.py`:
- **MoE & auxiliary loss training gradient parity (`_normalize_loss_output`, `diff_wrapper`)**: When `include_aux_losses=True` (enabled in `diff_wrapper` for training; disabled in `_eval_kernel` so evaluation `loss` remains cross-entropy-only), includes `(moe_lb_loss + indexer_loss + mtp_loss) * total_weights` (with explicit `None` guards) in `primary_loss.unreduced_sum`. Previously `diff_wrapper` differentiated `xent_sum` alone, giving **zero gradient** to `moe_lb_loss`, `indexer_loss`, and `mtp_loss`. At `gradient_accumulation_steps=1` this matches `pre_train/train.py`'s training loss (`12.924` vs `10.391` cross-entropy-only) and gradients; at `gradient_accumulation_steps > 1` the loss matches for equal-token micro-batches and auxiliary gradients are applied at full weight. (Init-time `logical_axis_rules` binding during model creation is handled upstream by #5383.)
- **Support `optimizer_memory_host_offload` (`_offload_optimizer_state_to_host`, `_compile_for_batch`, `_update_kernel`, `_zero1_sharding`)**: Offloads optimizer state leaves onto `pinned_host` shardings via `maxtext_utils_nnx.move_memory_to_host` before compiling, pulls them onto `device` via `jax.device_put` inside `_update_kernel` before `apply_gradients`, routes updated moments back to `pinned_host` via `update_out_shardings`, and preserves `memory_kind` across Zero-1 `_zero1_sharding` passes.
- **Respect `enable_checkpointing=False` (`_checkpoint_dir`)**: Returns `""` when `enable_checkpointing=False` so Orbax `CheckpointManager` creation is cleanly skipped.
- **Skip non-scalar auxiliary outputs in metrics (`record_metrics`)**: Skips `None` entries, NNX `intermediate_outputs` (sow activations), and `(tuple, list)` entries (e.g. `moe_bias_updates` and `mtp_moe_bias_updates`) so `MetricsBuffer` only receives scalar/array metrics.

2. `src/maxtext/experimental/maxtext_engine/train.py`:
- **Guard checkpoint restore/save behind `config.enable_checkpointing`**: Only calls `engine.restore_checkpoint()` and `engine.save_checkpoint(metadata=None)` when `config.enable_checkpointing` is enabled.
- **Full-step XProf profiling parity**: Disables `engine._profiler` (`do_not_profile = True`, which only wraps individual `fwd_bwd` micro-steps) and wraps the outer loop with MaxText's `Profiler(config, offset_step=start_step)` and `jax.profiler.StepTraceAnnotation("train", step_num=step)` so `skip_first_n_steps_for_profiler` and `profiler_steps` capture full optimizer steps (`N * fwd_bwd + 1 * update`) identically to `pre_train/train.py`.
- **Step wall-clock synchronization**: Calls `engine._throttler.wait_for_all()` after `engine.update()` so asynchronous device execution and metric flushes complete before measuring `step_time_s` or closing the XProf profiler window.
- **Throughput & TFLOP/s logging**: Precomputes `tokens_per_step` and per-device TFLOPs to log `TFLOP/s/device`, `train_step_time_ms`, and `Tokens/s/device` every step, and binds `with logical_axis_rules(config.logical_axis_rules):` in `main()`.

3. `tests/post_training/unit/maxtext_engine_test.py`:
- Adds unit tests for `optimizer_memory_host_offload` (`pinned_host` placement/idempotence and step math parity), training vs. eval auxiliary loss handling (`include_aux_losses`), `record_metrics` filtering, `enable_checkpointing=False` `_checkpoint_dir` gating, and `_zero1_sharding` `memory_kind` preservation.

title: DiLoCo sharding: split a mesh along the `diloco` axis and strip that axis from logical rules.
body:
DiLoCo sharding: split a mesh along the `diloco` axis and strip that axis from logical rules.

Threaded (non-SPMD) streaming DiLoCo trains each DiLoCo replica as a separate
program on its own slice of the `diloco` mesh axis. These two helpers derive that
per-replica view from the global one:

-   `split_mesh_along_axis(mesh, axis_name="diloco")` returns one submesh per index
    of `axis_name`, without that axis and with the remaining axes and axis types in
    their original order, so any PartitionSpec that doesn't mention the axis stays
    valid on every submesh.
-   `remove_mesh_axis_from_rules(rules, axis_name="diloco")` drops the axis from the
    physical axes of every logical-axis rule. Rules that map only to that axis are
    removed, so the logical axis falls through to its next matching rule.

No existing callers change.

Testing: new `tests/unit/diloco_sharding_test.py` (submesh devices per index, missing
axis error, rule stripping).

title: DiLoCo: fragment extraction/application and outer step for threaded streaming DiLoCo.
body:
DiLoCo: fragment extraction/application and outer step for threaded streaming DiLoCo.

Adds `trainers/diloco/utils/fragment_transfer.py`: the jitted pieces a threaded
DiLoCo learner uses to extract one parameter fragment per sync step, move it to the
host-side syncer, and apply the synced result a few steps later. Nothing uses it yet.
The trainer comes in a follow-up CL.

-   A *transfer fragment* is a dict `key -> 1-D jax.Array`, keyed like
    `FragmentedTreeManipulator.get_flat_fragment`. Each leaf is flattened
    shard-locally with `jax.shard_map`, so extract/apply never move data between
    chips and host transfers only see 1-D arrays. Leaves whose fragment shape isn't
    divisible by their sharding fall back to a global reshape.
-   `FragmentTransfer(manipulator, params, alpha)`: one jitted extract and one
    jitted apply for all layer fragments (the fragment index is a traced argument),
    plus a pair for fragment 0. `apply` pins its output shardings to the live
    parameters and donates them, so the train step sees unchanged shardings and the
    scanned layer stacks are updated in place. `alpha` implements
    `communication_overlapping_alpha`. Layer fragments must form an arithmetic
    progression (sequential or strided assignment), which is checked at construction.
-   `move_fragment(fragment, mesh)`: one batched `device_put` that keeps each
    array's PartitionSpec.
-   `nesterov_outer_step(...)`: float32 Nesterov outer step on the pseudo-gradient
    `outer - mean(learner fragments)`, equivalent to
    `optax.sgd(lr, momentum, nesterov=True)`.

Testing: new `tests/unit/diloco_fragment_transfer_test.py` on 8 CPU devices:
extract->apply moves exactly one fragment (sequential/strided, bucketized or not),
transfer arrays are 1-D and shard-local, apply keeps shardings and donates, alpha
interpolation, non-arithmetic layer assignment is rejected, `move_fragment` keeps
specs, and the outer step matches optax and keeps dtypes.

title: Fix MaxTextTrainingEngine optimizer host offload, logical_axis_rules ownership, and fp32 grad accumulation

title: DiLoCo fragmenter: optionally bucketize large non-scanned params across layer fragments.
body:
DiLoCo fragmenter: optionally bucketize large non-scanned params across layer fragments.

Streaming DiLoCo always puts every non-scanned parameter (embedding, output head,
final norm) into fragment 0, so the step that syncs fragment 0 moves far more data
than the layer steps: for Qwen3-8B the 151936-row embedding and head together
exceed a decoder layer several times over. With `diloco_bucketize_non_scanned`, every non-scanned leaf
with ndim >= 2 and at least `num_diloco_fragments - 1` rows is split row-wise
across the layer fragments, so each sync step moves about the same amount of data.

-   `FragmentedTreeManipulator` routes leaves through one keyed path
    (`_iter_keyed_leaves`) and describes each bucketized leaf with a `BucketSpec`
    (`chunk_size`, `remainder`). Flat fragment keys use the `#bucket` and
    `#remainder` suffixes; the remainder rows stay in fragment 0.
-   New config field `diloco_bucketize_non_scanned` (default `False`). With the
    default, fragment contents and the SPMD streaming DiLoCo trajectory are unchanged.
-   Both runners build their fragments with this class: the SPMD runner
    (`diloco.py`) and the threaded (MPMD) runner that a follow-up CL adds. The flag
    therefore works with either. SPMD needs no other change: it picks the fragment
    with `lax.switch` over static indices, so every branch has static row ranges.

Testing:

-   New `tests/unit/diloco_fragmenter_test.py`:
    -   Fragmenter: extract/apply round trips (bucketized or not, sequential or
        strided layer assignment), every parameter lands in exactly one fragment,
        bucket/remainder keys and shapes, off by default, a leading replica dim, and
        `ShapeDtypeStruct` leaves.
    -   SPMD sync path: running `spmd_diloco_sync.synchronize_fragment_state` once
        per fragment inside a 2-replica `drjax.program` must equal one full-tree
        Nesterov outer step (params and momentum trace), with and without
        bucketization. Injecting a replica-axis slicing bug into the bucket
        extraction makes the bucketized case fail.
-   `test_streaming_diloco_two_slices_bucketized` in `tests/integration/diloco_test.py`:
    AOT compile of the SPMD streaming step with bucketization for a 2x tpu7x-8
    topology.
-   CPU SPMD streaming DiLoCo smoke run (8 steps, 2 replicas, 3 fragments): the losses
    with the flag off match the pre-change code at every step (7.462 -> 7.399).
-   Hardware: SPMD streaming DiLoCo, 2x v6e-8, Qwen3-8B, 37 fragments (one per step),
    tau=5, 200 steps, synthetic data, run with the flag off and on. Both exit 0 with
    no errors and finite losses at every step.
    -   Losses match to the logged 3 decimals through step 6 and diverge from step 7
        on. The first synced fragment is applied at the end of step 5.
    -   Mean loss over steps 150-199: 6.917 (off) vs 6.944 (on).
    -   Wall time over steps 20-199: 1.378 s/step (off) vs 1.389 s/step (on).

title: Fix: Numeric divergence between the mHC layer and its Pallas kernel
body:
Bug report: https://github.com/AI-Hypercomputer/maxtext/issues/5195

# Description

**Motivation:**
The reference path had its own `mapping` helper that cast `alpha_scale` and
`beta` down to `self.dtype` before computing `sigmoid(alpha_scale * h + beta)`,
while the Pallas path called `common.compute_sigmoid_gate`, which keeps the
scale and bias in float32. With `dtype: bfloat16` the two branches therefore
gated on different numbers, so toggling `use_mhc_pallas_kernel` changed the
layer's output beyond accumulation noise.

**Implementation:**
Drop `ManifoldConstrainedHyperConnections.mapping` and call the shared
`compute_sigmoid_gate` from both pre- and post-mapping, casting the float32
result back to `self.dtype` so the following GEMM is unchanged. Export the
helper from `maxtext.kernels.mhc` so the layer can reach it.

**Tests:**
- `test_pallas_kernel_matches_reference_path` runs the same weights through
  both branches and asserts they agree; the `_tpu` variant repeats it against
  the Mosaic-compiled kernel instead of interpret mode.
- `test_sigmoid_gate_computes_in_float32` pins the helper's precision directly,
  since the end-to-end comparison cannot resolve a bfloat16 regression there.
- Fold the four copies of the interpret-mode kernel patching into the
  `_interpreted_mhc_kernel` context manager, and the repeated module/MLP
  construction into `_build_mhc_and_mlp`.

title: Make three silent failures in the Raiden training path visible
body:
# Description


Each change targets a failure that produced no usable signal at the point of cause: weights that never transfer, metadata that fails in another process, and a performance cliff recorded only in a docstring.

unscan_layers had no tests, and it is the piece that decides whether trainer and sampler tensor names agree. Both sides name tensors with jax.tree_util.keystr, and nothing cross-checks the two sets: raiden_handler._validate_metadata only validates one manifest's internal consistency (mesh rank, duplicate variable/layer keys, sharding specs). A naming error therefore surfaces as weights that silently never transfer. Two cases pin non-obvious invariants: unscan_layers returns a plain nested dict while the sampler binds an nnx.State, and keystr renders those identically only because the transform rewraps leaves in nnx.Param -- dropping that rewrap would rename every tensor ("['k']" vs "['k'].value"); and an already-unscanned state must raise, since without that guard it would return unchanged and bind under scanned names.

prepare_weight_sync returned empty metadata on two paths: a missing raiden_synchronizer (warning-level) and an unrecognised staging_transport (no log at all). Neither is silent end to end -- WeightSyncCoordinator rejects an empty side -- but the failure lands far from the cause, surfacing in another process as "metadata collection returned an empty side", a count that never names the missing module or the bad transport. The import case is the common one rather than a corner: raiden_synchronizer ships only on tunix's Raiden branch, so any released tunix takes it. Both now raise where the cause is known, with the ImportError chained so the traceback keeps the module name. Because staging_transport defaults to "raiden", this also reaches callers that never asked for it, so the engine e2e test now probes for the synchronizer the way the engine does -- exercising the real staging path where Raiden exists and the documented failure where it does not.

_batch_data_shardings falls back to replicating the batch dimension when it does not divide the batch axis's mesh size. That is correct -- every device along the axis computes the whole micro-batch -- but it costs N times the work a sharded one would do there. An invisible performance cliff is harder to notice than a wrong number, because XLA's caching can make it look like nothing worse than a slow run; the file already warns once per instance when a signature half cannot be compared, and this extends that treatment. Warned once per instance rather than per leaf, since the check runs under a tree_map over every loss input and they normally share a batch dim. A sequence-packed micro-batch is always size 1 and has no alternative, so the message says the fallback may well be deliberate.

Verification. The unscan suite has teeth: renaming the emitted key from layers_{i} to layer_{i} fails 5 of its 11 tests, including the name-equality one. Marked post_training and left in tests/unit, which is already in cpu-post-training-unit's path list, so the marker alone routes it -- tests/ and tests/integration are not in that list, which is how the engine tests once ended up collected by no job at all; collection confirms 11 tests in cpu-post-training-unit and 0 in cpu-unit. The staging and sharding tests fail without their respective changes. The sharding tests stub both the data spec and the axis size: a single-device test mesh returns None in the batch position, making the branch unreachable as configured, and an earlier draft asserted `spec[0] is None` and passed without running the code under test at all.

title: Trim small pre-GMM routing and ragged sort operations in MoE RoE.
body:
Trim small pre-GMM routing and ragged sort operations in MoE RoE.

In Ring-of-Experts (`use_ring_of_experts=True`) with `use_ragged_sort=True`, the routing and sorting window before the first MoE grouped matmul (and its backward counterpart) previously incurred extra collective latency, a SparseCore-offloaded index gather, and three redundant TensorCore sorts per layer:

* Span the routed-bias `expert_counts` `jax.lax.psum` across all batch axes (including the expert-parallel axis) and divide out `replication_factor=num_ep` in `calculate_load_balance_updates`. In RoE, every EP shard routes the same all-gathered batch and computes identical token counts. Including the EP axis allows XLA to use a multi-dimensional all-reduce and fuse it with the whole-mesh `has_overflow` `psum` instead of running a separate sub-mesh reduction over non-EP axes only, while exact integer division by `replication_factor` recovers the global counts and keeps summed counts within `int32`.
* Derive `token_indices_sorted` in `ring_ragged_sort` via `(topk_argsort_indices // topk).astype(jnp.int32)` instead of `jnp.arange(num_tokens_local).repeat(topk)[topk_argsort_indices]`. Because flat slot `j` belongs to token `j // topk`, integer division avoids materializing the repeated range and eliminates a full-size SparseCore gather before `ragged_gather`.
* Replace `jnp.argsort` permutation inversions (`topk_argsort_revert_indices` in `ring_ragged_sort` forward and `idx_inv` in `ring_ragged_unsort` backward) with `_inverse_permutation`, which scatters `jnp.arange(n)` into zeros using `.at[perm].add(..., unique_indices=True, mode="promise_in_bounds")` so XLA can offload the $O(N)$ inverse permutation to SparseCore instead of running a full radix sort on TensorCore.
* Replace the boolean `jnp.argsort(~valid_rows_mask_2d, stable=True)` in `ragged_gather_reduce_v2._preprocess` with a prefix-sum destination computation (`jnp.cumsum`) followed by a single unique-index scatter-add.
* Add unit tests for `replication_factor` in `calculate_load_balance_updates`, `_inverse_permutation`, and `ragged_gather_reduce_v2._preprocess`.

title: MoE: dense custom VJP for the router top-k selection (no scatter in the backward)
body:
<!-- BODY START -->
`deepseek_routing` takes the top-k routing weights with `jnp.take_along_axis(pre_bias_logits, top_k_indices, axis=-1)`.
Its transpose is a scatter-add of the `[tokens, k]` cotangent into `[tokens, num_experts]`, which XLA lowers on the TPU
to an element-serial `scatter_fusion`. The backward runs two of these per MoE layer (one per routing chunk); an earlier
profile of this model put them at about 1.6 ms per call.

This PR adds `router_topk_matmul_vjp` (default `false`). With it on, the gather goes through
`take_along_last_axis_dense_vjp`, a `jax.custom_vjp` whose forward is the same `take_along_axis` and whose backward
builds the dense gradient as a one-hot compare-select sum over the k slots,
`dx[..., e] = sum_k g[..., k] * (indices[..., k] == e)`. Top-k indices are distinct per token, so each output element
receives at most one term and the gradient of the op is bitwise equal to the scatter-add. In the full model the dense
result joins the other gate-logit gradient terms in a different fusion, so the summed gradient may differ by fp
reassociation. The config read uses `getattr(config, "router_topk_matmul_vjp", False)` so configs that do not declare
the field (e.g. `DummyConfig` in `router_replay_test.py`) keep the existing path.

### Measured effect

512 chips (one 8x8x8 v7x slice), DeepSeek-V3 671B MLPerf recipe, seed 1234, flag on vs off. Both runs were profiled
(steps 25-26); steady step is the mean of steps 21-42 excluding the profile steps.

| | flag off | flag on |
|---|---|---|
| steady step (s) | 3.829 | 3.675 (-4.0%) |
| `scatter_fusion` time in the profiled window (ms) | 748.9 | 0 |
| eval target reached at (samples) | 58368 | 55296 |

Loss agrees within 0.001 through step 16, then drifts by up to 0.06 (the flag-on run lower), consistent with the
reassociation above. One seed each; an unprofiled multi-seed confirmation has not run yet.

Compiled program (AOT, same config): with the flag off it is identical to the program before this change; with it on
there are 4 fewer scatter ops, code -3.9 MB, temps -2.2 MB, arguments and outputs unchanged, and the same dot count.

### Usage

Add `router_topk_matmul_vjp=true` to the run's config overrides (DeepSeek routing only; default `false`).

### Tests

Two new tests in `tests/unit/moe_test.py`:
`test_take_along_last_axis_dense_vjp_matches_take_along_axis` (forward and gradient bitwise equal to
`take_along_axis` for top-k indices; the lowered gradient contains no scatter) and
`test_deepseek_routing_topk_matmul_vjp` (`deepseek_routing` indices, weights and gradients bitwise equal with the flag
on and off).

On CPU (`JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu`, `pytest -n 16 -m "not tpu_only and not gpu_only"`) `tests/unit/moe_test.py` and

title: MoE: first-phase ragged buffer, dropless fallback and precompiled replay/eval programs
body:
## What and why

With `retry_when_tokens_dropped`, a train step whose ragged buffer overflows is discarded and replayed with the dropless
program. The steps right after a (re)start overflow most often, because routing is least balanced there. Each such step
then pays for a normal attempt, a discard and a dropless replay, and before this change the dropless program was also
compiled lazily inside the timed loop on its first use. We would rather give those early steps a buffer that is large
enough, keep the retry as a safety net, and compile every program the loop can run before the loop starts.

`retry_dropless_first_steps=N` runs the steps with `step - start_step < N` without the normal attempt. With
`first_phase_ragged_buffer_factor=0` they run the dropless program directly. With a factor > 0 they run a first-phase
program, which is the normal train program with `RoutedMoE.ragged_buffer_factor_override` set to that factor. It keeps a
finite (larger) buffer together with the normal remat policy and token chunking, so it costs much less per step than the
dropless program. A first-phase step that still overflows is replayed with the dropless program, exactly as a normal step
is. Validation requires `retry_when_tokens_dropped=True`, and for the first-phase factor also `ragged_buffer_factor > 0`
and a factor at least as large as `ragged_buffer_factor`.

`eval_ragged_buffer_factor` gives the eval program its own ragged buffer factor through the same per-graphdef override.
`RoutedMoE.effective_ragged_buffer_factor()` returns the override when it is > 0 and `config.ragged_buffer_factor`
otherwise, and every former read of `config.ragged_buffer_factor` in moe.py goes through it. It is not supported with
`te_moe_block`.

When `retry_when_tokens_dropped` is set, setup now compiles the dropless program, the first-phase program (when enabled)
and the eval program ahead of time next to the train program (`build_dropless_graphdef`, `build_first_phase_graphdef`,
`build_eval_graphdef`, `aot_compile_step`), so no compilation happens in the timed loop.

`log_required_ragged_buffer_factor` is a probe for choosing these factors. Each RoutedMoE computes, from the per-expert
counts the overflow check already uses, the smallest ragged buffer factor for which its shard would not have dropped
tokens, takes the max over the mesh (one float32 scalar max all-reduce per MoE layer and token chunk) and logs one
`REQUIRED_RBF step=... max=... per_layer=[...] program=...` line per train program run. The value is read on the host,
so it adds a device-to-host fetch per step. It is off by default and meant for tuning runs.

The change also fixes the replay remat override. The dropless graphdef set `remat_policy_override = "full"` only on
modules named `Decoder`, which matches nothing for `NNXDecoder`, so the replay ran with the normal remat policy.
`build_dropless_graphdef` matches any module that exposes `get_remat_policy()`. #5362 made the same fix inline in
`train_loop` and has since merged to main; on main this change replaces that inline block with the helper (the only
rebase conflict, see below).

Every new option is off by default, and without the flags the training loop takes the same branches as before.

## Knobs

| option | default | recommended (MLPerf DSv3, 512 chips) |
|---|---|---|
| `retry_dropless_first_steps` | 0 (off) | 20 |
| `first_phase_ragged_buffer_factor` | 0 (off; first steps run dropless) | 4.75 |
| `ragged_buffer_factor` (existing) | -1 | 3.0 |
| `eval_ragged_buffer_factor` (from main, #5377) | -1 (dropless worst-case buffer under eval axis rules) | 4 |
| `log_required_ragged_buffer_factor` | false | false (tuning only) |

The recommendation rests on the probe: the baseline runs below logged a largest required factor of 4.62 in steps 0-19
across three seeds, and the fp30 and fp35 runs logged at most 2.80 after step 20.

## Results

Setup: 512 chips (one 8x8x8 slice), v4.0 team image with this change's source files overlaid
(`integrate_v2:mlperf61v4-stack4`), profiler off, seeds 1234, 4321 and 777. The baseline ("today") runs 10 dropless steps
and then `ragged_buffer_factor=3.5`. The new setting ("fp30") runs 20 first-phase steps at 4.75 and then
`ragged_buffer_factor=3.0`. Both arms have `eval_ragged_buffer_factor=4` and ran with the required-factor probe on, so both
include its per-step fetch. Steady is the mean of steps 21-42; e2e is run_stop - run_start. All per-seed numbers are
measured; medians and comparisons are derived.

| seed | arm | steady s/step (21-42) | replays (step) | target step (loss) | e2e s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1234 | today | 3.8896 | none | 56 (3.592) | 308.8 |
| 1234 | fp30 | 3.8311 | none | 54 (3.597) | 281.1 |
| 4321 | today | 3.8871 | 4 (11, 12, 18, 19) | 54 (3.595) | 320.9 |
| 4321 | fp30 | 3.8297 | none | 58 (3.599) | 318.9 |
| 777 | today | 3.8883 | none | 53 (3.600) | 293.7 |
| 777 | fp30 | 3.8288 | none | 54 (3.591) | 281.1 |

The 3-seed median e2e is 308.8 s today and 281.1 s with fp30. A first-phase step at 4.75 takes 4.16-4.20 s against
5.70-5.76 s for a dropless step, and no fp30 run replayed at any step, so seed 4321's four late replays (steps 11, 12, 18
and 19, which overflowed rbf 3.5 after the dropless window) are gone. After step 20, the 3.0 buffer runs roughly 57-60 ms
per step faster than 3.5 on every seed.

The evidence has clear limits. It is n=3 seeds on one slice size. Target steps scatter from 53 to 59 across all arms we
ran, so an e2e comparison still carries that scatter (e.g. on seed 4321 fp30 reached the target four steps later than
today and the e2e margin is only 2.0 s). The per-step numbers (first-phase step time, steady step time, replay count) are
the more direct measure of the change. We have not measured other slice sizes or the probe-off setting at these factors.


Scale note: the recommended first-phase settings (20 steps at 4.75, then 3.0) were tuned at 512 and 1024 chips, where they gave zero replays on three seeds. At 2048 chips (one 8x16x16 slice, GBS 4096) the same schedule ran at 4.157 s/step (-82 ms against the dropless first phase) but replayed at steps 6 and 30, so larger batches need their own probe run to set the two buffer factors.

## Tests

CPU, inside the v4.0 team image (sha256:59fdf0f1...) with the branch's `src/` and `tests/` mounted:
`pytest -n 16 -m "not tpu_only and not gpu_only"` on tests/unit/{moe, configs_value, configs, pyconfig, train_utils,
train_nnx, pre_train_loss_mask}_test.py gives 283 passed, 136 subtests passed (69.1 s). New tests cover the first-phase
program inside the window, the normal program after it, the dropless replay of an overflowing first-phase step, the
`REQUIRED_RBF` log line, and the required factor against the `get_ragged_buffer_size` boundary.

`pre-commit run --files <changed files>` passes (codespell, pylint, pyink, yamllint) on the branch and on the branch rebased
onto origin/main (1db7b218a). That rebase has one conflict, in `train_loop` of train.py, where #5362's inline dropless
graphdef block meets the `build_dropless_graphdef` call; taking this change's side resolves it.

Rebased onto main after #5377 (b33d0f687), which added its own `eval_ragged_buffer_factor` and `RoutedMoE.get_ragged_buffer_factor()`. title: c4_mlperf: read and cache each host's own eval batch once
body:
## c4_mlperf: read and cache each host's own eval batch once

On the MLPerf DeepSeek eval split (c4/en:3.0.9: 2048 tfrecord files of one pre-tokenized 32,768-token example each, so one example per host at 128 hosts), every eval made every host read the eval files from GCS again. Three things combined. The eval dataset is sharded after reading, so host i reads files 0..i to find its first example, and the tfds interleave and the prefetch read further ahead. The in-memory `cache()` covers the host's whole shard (16 examples) while the eval loop consumes `num_batches` (= 1) batch and breaks, and a partially read cache is discarded when the iterator is reset, so it never completed. And the eval iterator was built twice per eval (the explicit `reset()` in train.py, then again in `MultiHostDataLoadIterator.__iter__`).

Since the eval is a collective, the slowest host sets the eval time. In one 512-chip wave we saw evals of 7-55 s against a 1.5 s floor, only on the eval path, in wall-clock windows shared across runs, with one host blocking 18.5 s inside its pre-eval reset. The eval bucket served 10.9-19.4k req/s in the minutes of that wave against at most 1.35k req/s in the train-only minutes before it (which of the two drives the other is open).

### Changes

1. `preprocess_eval_dataset`: `take(num_batches)` before `cache()`, so the first eval completes the cache and later evals read from host memory. The eval loop never consumes more than `num_batches` batches, so the batches it sees are unchanged.
2. `make_c4_mlperf_eval_iterator`: `shard_in_read=True` when every file of the split holds exactly one example and there are at least as many files as loading hosts (checked from the split's file instructions in dataset_info). Host i then opens only files i, i + n, ..., which select the same examples in the same order as sharding after reading. Other layouts (e.g. c4/en:3.0.1 with many examples per file) keep sharding after reading, since sharding by file would change which examples a host gets.
3. `MultiHostDataLoadIterator.__iter__` skips the rebuild when `reset()` was just called and nothing has been read since. The explicit reset in train.py is the one correctness depends on, because `_ReorderedDataIterator` and `RemoteIteratorWrapper` return `self` from `__iter__` without resetting. The reset in `__iter__` stays for plain for loops (the `test_for_loop_repeatable` tests).

### Tests

`EvalReadsOwnFilesOnceTest` writes a local split of 2048 one-example files and counts the files the tfds reader reads, for hosts 0, 5, 64 and 127 of 128. The eval batch (all six features) is identical between the old read path and the new one on every eval, the first eval reads only the host's own files, later evals read none, and one eval is exactly `num_batches` long. It sleeps 0.5 s between evals to stand in for the train step, during which the prefetch completes the truncated cache; on a heavily loaded runner that window is the timing dependence of the test. A train_utils test checks that `reset()` followed by a for loop builds one local iterator.

On the real split (read-only, CPU), the eval batches of hosts 0, 5, 64 and 127 are byte-identical before and after the change, and host 127 reads its own 16 files on the first eval and 0 files on the next three. `pytest -m "not tpu_only and not gpu_only"` on the c4 / input pipeline tests and the train / config / MoE tests: the same 17 grain tests fail before and after for lack of local gcsfuse data; everything else passes.

### Validation on hardware

Two 512-chip runs of the MLPerf DeepSeek recipe with this change (same seed and flags as a run without it, images differing only in these two files): the first three evals take 1.58 / 1.45 / 1.45 s in the mllog against 3.70 / 4.42 / 3.67 s without the change, and every later eval takes 1.43-1.56 s (20 evals, none over 3 s). Train step time (3.666 vs 3.667 s) and loss (within 0.055 through step 42) are unchanged. Neither run showed the multi-second eval stalls that appeared in 7 of the earlier runs.

title: Restore custom NNX collections in model_creation_utils.from_pretrained
body:
`from_pretrained` has its own Orbax restore path, separate from `checkpointing.load_params_from_path` (fixed in #5226). For Linen-layout checkpoints (`params/params/...`) it had the same bug #5226 fixed for the training path: weights promoted to custom `nnx.Variable` subclasses (`MoEBiasVar`, `Tid2EidVar`) were never restored.

Two defects:

1. Request built at the wrong path. The whole model state was requested under `params/params`, but converters such as the DeepSeek-V4 one write each custom collection as a sibling (`params/MoEBiasVar/...`, `params/Tid2EidVar/...`). Custom-collection leaves were requested at paths that do not exist on disk.

2. Restored collections dropped. After restore only `restored["params"]["params"]` was kept, discarding every other collection.

Fix:

- Group abstract leaves by collection via `variable_name_from_type` and build one restore target + restore_args per collection present on disk. Collections on disk that the model does not define are skipped.
- Merge all restored collections into a single tree (`_deep_merge_dicts`) before alignment to model shapes.
- When freeing device memory ahead of restore, skip variables whose collection is not being restored, so they keep their initialized buffer instead of becoming dangling deleted arrays that fail at first use.

The NNX-layout checkpoint branch is unchanged.

Affects callers of `from_pretrained`, including
`tests/utils/forward_pass_logit_checker.py`. This loader was used for the DeepSeek-V4 scanned/unscanned forward-pass logit checks on v5p-32 (median KL ~0.012 vs HF goldens, max KL 0.41/37 respectively).
